q: A developer uses GitHub Copilot to generate a function. Before merging, what is the most important step according to responsible AI principles?
opts: Accept the suggestion immediately to save time
Share the suggestion with the team for a vote
Reject all AI suggestions to maintain code ownership
Review and validate the AI-generated code before committing
exp: Responsible AI use requires that humans always review and validate AI output. AI should never have the final say without human oversight.

q: Which two of the following are key principles of responsible AI use with GitHub Copilot? (Select 2)
opts: Transparency — being clear about how AI decisions are made
Automation — letting AI make final decisions autonomously
Speed — always prioritising the fastest suggestion
Fairness — ensuring AI does not reinforce existing biases
exp: Fairness and transparency are two of the core responsible AI pillars. 'Automation without oversight' and pure speed are not responsible AI principles.

q: Which phrase best describes a key limitation of GitHub Copilot that developers must account for?
opts: It may produce plausible-looking code that is actually incorrect or insecure
It always incorporates the latest security patches and CVE mitigations
It requires a persistent internet connection to function even for cached completions
It only generates code in the two most common programming languages
exp: Copilot can generate code that looks correct but contains bugs or security vulnerabilities. Developers must validate output.

q: A Copilot suggestion subtly reinforces a biased outcome in a classification model. Which responsible AI principle is most directly at stake?
opts: Accountability
Fairness
Transparency
Security
exp: Fairness addresses whether AI outputs perpetuate or amplify biases. The exam often tests the distinction between fairness and inclusion.

q: Which of the following best describes 'accountability' in responsible AI use with GitHub Copilot?
opts: Organisations must publish a public disclosure of all AI-assisted code in each release
The developer who commits AI-generated code is responsible for reviewing and owning it
AI models bear legal liability for defects in the code they generate
GitHub automatically logs all accepted suggestions for retrospective legal review
exp: Accountability means the developer who accepts and commits AI-generated code owns it — both legally and professionally.

q: Which two strategies help mitigate the risks of AI-generated code in a production codebase? (Select 2)
opts: Always run AI-generated code through automated tests and code review
Trust Copilot to handle edge cases without manual verification
Disable linting tools so Copilot suggestions appear faster
Apply security scanning to catch potential vulnerabilities in suggestions
exp: Running tests/code review and applying security scanning are concrete mitigation strategies. Disabling linting and skipping verification increase risk.

q: A developer notices Copilot consistently suggests code that uses deprecated APIs. What is the responsible course of action?
opts: Accept the suggestions anyway since Copilot is usually right
Disable Copilot permanently for the project
Validate and update the suggestions to use current APIs before committing
Report the issue and wait for GitHub to fix the model
exp: Developers are responsible for validating AI output. Suggestions referencing outdated APIs should be updated before committing — this is a core human-in-the-loop responsibility.

q: What does 'transparency' mean in the context of responsible AI use with GitHub Copilot?
opts: All accepted suggestions are logged and made publicly available for community review
Developers are open about when and how AI was used to generate code in their workflow
Copilot displays the exact training examples it used to generate each suggestion
GitHub publishes the full source code and training data of the underlying AI model
exp: Transparency in responsible AI means being open about how AI tools are used in development processes — e.g. disclosing AI assistance to teammates or reviewers.

q: Which of the following is a potential harm of over-relying on GitHub Copilot without human review?
opts: Copilot begins rejecting further suggestions after a usage threshold is exceeded
Developers may unknowingly introduce security vulnerabilities that bypass code review
Copilot automatically refactors the codebase when it detects overuse patterns
Suggestions will always be syntactically valid, so at least compilation is guaranteed
exp: Over-reliance without review risks introducing bugs, security holes, or biased logic that the developer would otherwise catch.

q: How does GitHub Copilot address the risk of generating harmful or offensive content in code comments or strings?
opts: It applies a toxicity filter as part of its prompt processing pipeline
It relies entirely on the developer's judgement with no automated safeguard
It blocks all natural-language content and only generates code
It requires manual content review by GitHub staff before showing suggestions
exp: GitHub Copilot's proxy pipeline includes a toxicity filter that screens both input and output for harmful content before suggestions are displayed.

q: A company wants to prevent developer code from being used to train GitHub Copilot's AI models. Which plan is the minimum required?
opts: GitHub Copilot Individual
GitHub Copilot Business
GitHub Copilot Pro
GitHub Copilot Free
exp: Business and Enterprise plans include the policy that user prompts are not retained or used for model training. Free and Pro plans do not guarantee this at an organisational level.

q: An enterprise wants centralised policy management, audit log access, and content exclusion enforcement across all repositories. Which plan supports all of these?
opts: GitHub Copilot Business
GitHub Copilot Individual
GitHub Copilot Pro
GitHub Copilot Free
exp: Business (and Enterprise) plans include organisation-level policy management, audit logs, and content exclusion enforcement.

q: Which two features are available in GitHub Copilot Enterprise but NOT in GitHub Copilot Business? (Select 2)
opts: Fine-tuned models customised on your organisation's private code
Duplication detection / public code matching toggle
Organisation-wide content exclusions
Copilot Chat on github.com with context of the organisation's codebase
exp: Enterprise adds Copilot Chat on github.com with org-wide context awareness, and fine-tuned models on private code. Business already includes content exclusions and duplication detection.

q: A developer asks: 'How can I ensure suggestions generated for me are never used to improve Copilot's models for other users?' What is the correct answer?
opts: Add a .copilotignore file to the repository
Disable telemetry in the IDE extension
Switch to GitHub Copilot Business or Enterprise
Enable the duplication filter in IDE settings
exp: Opting out of training data collection is a Business/Enterprise plan policy enforced organisation-wide. IDE-level settings do not control this.

q: A startup with 10 developers uses GitHub Copilot Business. They now need Copilot to answer questions using context from their internal wiki and private codebase on github.com. What should they do?
opts: Enable the knowledge base feature in Business settings
Add a copilot-instructions.md to each repository
Use GitHub Actions to sync context to Copilot
Upgrade to GitHub Copilot Enterprise
exp: Enterprise adds the ability to index private repositories and internal content for use in Copilot Chat on github.com. This is not available in Business.

q: Which plan allows an organisation to manage Copilot subscriptions using the REST API?
opts: All plans including Free
Copilot Free only
Copilot Pro only
Copilot Business and Enterprise
exp: The REST API for managing Copilot seats and subscriptions is available for Business and Enterprise plan administrators.

q: A CTO asks: 'Under which Copilot plan can we enforce that developers may only use Copilot in approved IDEs?' What is the correct answer?
opts: GitHub Copilot Pro
This cannot be enforced on any plan
GitHub Copilot Free
GitHub Copilot Business or Enterprise
exp: Organisation-level feature availability controls (including restricting which IDEs can use Copilot) are available only on Business and Enterprise plans.

q: Which two scenarios would require upgrading from Copilot Business to Copilot Enterprise? (Select 2)
opts: The organisation wants Copilot Chat on github.com to reference private repository context
The organisation wants to enforce content exclusions org-wide
The organisation wants to customise the AI model on their own codebase
The organisation wants to enable the public code matching filter
exp: Enterprise-only features are: Copilot Chat on github.com with private context awareness, and fine-tuning the model on private code. Content exclusions and public code matching are Business features.

q: A developer wants to ensure their code contributed to an open-source project is never stored by GitHub for AI training. Which plan feature addresses this?
opts: Pro plan incognito mode
Business/Enterprise plan data retention policy
Individual plan privacy toggle in IDE
Free plan telemetry opt-out per user
exp: Data retention and training exclusion policies are enforced at the organisation level under Business/Enterprise. Individual opt-outs via IDE settings are unreliable for this guarantee.

q: What is the key difference between the Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise audit log capabilities?
opts: Enterprise audit logs include Copilot Chat on github.com activity; Business logs are limited to IDE events
Enterprise retains logs for 7 days; Business retains for 180 days
Business and Enterprise have identical audit logs
Business has no audit log; Enterprise does
exp: Enterprise extends audit log coverage to include Copilot Chat interactions on github.com, in addition to IDE-level events available in Business.

q: A developer adds exclusion rules in their repository's .github folder. What is the scope?
opts: Applies globally to the developer's IDE
Applies to all repositories in the organisation
Applies to all repositories owned by the same user
Applies only to the repository where the file exists
exp: Repository-level exclusion rules are scoped to that single repository only. Org-wide rules must be set in Organisation settings.

q: If a path is excluded at the Organisation level, and a developer's repository does NOT exclude that path, what happens?
opts: It depends on the user's plan tier
The repository setting overrides the organisation setting
The path remains excluded — exclusions are additive
The developer can override it locally in the IDE
exp: Exclusions are additive: if a path is excluded at any level, it remains excluded. A lower level cannot un-exclude what a higher level has blocked.

q: Which two statements about content exclusions in GitHub Copilot are correct? (Select 2)
opts: Organisation-level exclusions apply to all repositories in that organisation
Exclusions are additive — exclusion at any level persists
A developer can re-include org-excluded files using local IDE settings
A repository-level exclusion overrides an organisation-level exclusion
exp: Org exclusions propagate to all repos in the org. Exclusions are additive — lower levels cannot override higher-level blocks.

q: Where should an admin define exclusion rules to ensure they apply across every repository in an organisation?
opts: In the Organisation-level GitHub Copilot settings
In each repository's .github folder
In the Enterprise policy dashboard only
In each developer's IDE configuration
exp: Organisation-level GitHub Copilot settings is the correct place for rules that must apply organisation-wide.

q: A team defines a content exclusion at the local IDE level. Which statement is true?
opts: It is synced to the organisation's exclusion list automatically
It applies only within that developer's IDE session for that path
It applies to all users in the organisation
It overrides repository-level exclusions
exp: IDE-level exclusions apply only to that developer's local context. They do not affect other users and cannot override higher-level exclusions.

q: What effect does a content exclusion have on GitHub Copilot when a matching file is open?
opts: Copilot will not use the excluded file as context and will not suggest completions within it
Copilot generates suggestions but marks them as excluded
Copilot is disabled entirely for the whole project
The file is deleted from the repository
exp: Excluded files are ignored as context and receive no inline suggestions. Copilot does not use them to inform completions in other files either.

q: An organisation wants to prevent Copilot from suggesting code based on a proprietary algorithm file. What is the correct approach?
opts: Add the file to .gitignore
Encrypt the file so Copilot cannot read it
Define a content exclusion for that file path in Organisation-level Copilot settings
Set the file as read-only in the OS
exp: Content exclusions in Organisation-level Copilot settings are the correct mechanism to prevent specific files from being used as context or receiving suggestions.

q: A content exclusion is defined at both the repository level and the IDE level for the same path. Which two statements are true? (Select 2)
opts: If a third-level (org) exclusion is absent, the path is only excluded locally for that developer
Both exclusions apply — the path is excluded in both contexts
Exclusions from all levels combine — the path remains excluded regardless of which level defines it
The IDE-level exclusion is ignored since repository takes precedence
exp: Exclusions are additive across all levels. When a path is excluded at any level, it stays excluded. Multiple levels defining the same exclusion simply reinforce each other.

q: How long does GitHub retain Copilot audit log events for Business plan organisations by default?
opts: 90 days
30 days
180 days
7 days
exp: GitHub retains audit log events for 180 days for Business/Enterprise organisations. This specific retention period is frequently tested.

q: Which two of the following actions are captured in the GitHub Copilot audit log? (Select 2)
opts: A user enabling GitHub Copilot for their account
The exact code suggestions that were accepted by a developer
An admin changing the duplication detection policy
A developer's local IDE configuration changes
exp: Audit logs capture account/policy-level events. They do NOT record the content of specific code suggestions or local IDE settings.

q: An organisation wants to monitor which members are actively using GitHub Copilot and how frequently. Which tool should they use?
opts: GitHub Actions workflow logs — which record all automated tasks triggered by developers
The repository git commit history — filtered to identify commits containing AI-generated code
GitHub Copilot usage metrics in organisation settings — which show active seats and acceptance rates
The GitHub Copilot audit log — it records all user activity including suggestion frequency
exp: Usage metrics show seat usage and activity per member. Audit logs record policy/administrative events, not usage frequency.

q: An admin wants to know when a specific developer's Copilot seat was assigned. Where is this information found?
opts: The organisation audit log
The Copilot Chat history
The developer's personal GitHub settings
The repository's blame view
exp: Seat assignment events are recorded in the organisation audit log, which captures administrative actions like adding or removing Copilot access for members.

q: What data is NOT available in the GitHub Copilot usage metrics dashboard?
opts: Number of active Copilot seats
Number of suggestions accepted per developer
Acceptance rate trends over time
The specific code content of accepted suggestions
exp: Usage metrics show aggregate statistics (counts, rates, active seats). The actual code content of suggestions is never stored or displayed in dashboards.

q: For how long does GitHub retain prompts and suggestions from GitHub Copilot for Business by default?
opts: Prompts are not retained after the suggestion is returned — they are discarded
Prompts are retained for 28 days for abuse detection
Prompts are stored for 90 days and then anonymised
Prompts are stored indefinitely for model improvement
exp: For Business/Enterprise, prompts are not retained after the API call completes. They are used only to generate the suggestion and are then discarded.

q: What does the GitHub Copilot duplication filter (public code matching) do when enabled?
opts: Prevents users from copying code from public GitHub repos
Suppresses code suggestions that closely match code found in public repositories
Blocks suggestions that match publicly known security vulnerabilities
Scans your repo for duplicated functions
exp: The duplication filter suppresses suggestions that closely match publicly available code on GitHub, to reduce potential licence or IP concerns.

q: At which level can a Business plan administrator configure the public code matching (duplication) filter?
opts: Only at each developer's IDE settings
At the enterprise level only
At the organisation level in Copilot policy settings
Only at the repository level via .copilotignore
exp: Business plan admins configure public code matching at the organisation level. Individual users cannot override this if set by the org.

q: A developer working under a Business plan organisation has the duplication filter disabled in their IDE, but the organisation policy has it enabled. What happens?
opts: The organisation setting takes precedence — filter is enabled
Both settings apply simultaneously, causing a conflict error
The developer's IDE setting takes precedence — filter is disabled
The filter state is undefined until the next policy sync
exp: Organisation-level policies override individual IDE settings. This is consistent with the cascade logic: a lower level cannot override a higher-level policy.

q: What context does the duplication filter use to determine if a suggestion matches public code?
opts: The exact filename and directory structure
The repository's language settings
A semantic comparison of the suggested code block against public GitHub repositories
The developer's commit history
exp: The filter compares generated suggestions against an index of public code on GitHub to detect near-matches before surfacing the suggestion.

q: A developer provides three examples of input-output pairs before asking Copilot to generate a function. Which prompting technique is this?
opts: One-shot prompting
Zero-shot prompting
Role prompting
Few-shot prompting
exp: Few-shot prompting provides multiple examples (typically 2+) to guide the model. One-shot = 1 example; zero-shot = no examples.

q: A developer starts their Copilot Chat message with 'You are a senior security engineer reviewing this code for vulnerabilities.' What technique is this?
opts: Few-shot prompting
Role prompting
Zero-shot prompting
Chain-of-thought prompting
exp: Role prompting assigns a persona to the model to influence the style, expertise level, and perspective of its response.

q: Which statement best describes 'context' in GitHub Copilot's prompt processing?
opts: The current file, open tabs, chat history, and other signals assembled into the prompt
The repository's README and top-level configuration files only
Only the most recent message sent in the Copilot Chat window
Only the text in the current file that has been modified since the last save
exp: Context includes the active file, open/recent tabs, chat history, referenced files, and other signals Copilot uses to construct the actual prompt sent to the model.

q: Which two practices are considered best for crafting effective Copilot prompts? (Select 2)
opts: Always keep prompts as short as possible (one word)
Provide specific, detailed instructions with examples where possible
Include relevant context such as function signatures or existing code
Rely on Copilot to infer intent without any guidance
exp: Specificity and providing context (signatures, examples, related code) are best practices. Vague or minimal prompts reduce suggestion quality.

q: A developer asks Copilot to generate a function without providing any examples or context. Which prompting technique is this?
opts: One-shot prompting
Few-shot prompting
Zero-shot prompting
Role prompting
exp: Zero-shot prompting provides no examples — the model relies entirely on the instruction and its training. It often produces less targeted results than one-shot or few-shot.

q: Why is chat history important in GitHub Copilot Chat sessions?
opts: Chat history provides ongoing context that helps Copilot give relevant follow-up responses within the session
It replaces file context entirely once more than three messages have been exchanged
It is shared with all users in the organisation for collaborative context
It is stored permanently and used to retrain the model on the user's coding style
exp: Chat history is included as context in subsequent turns of a session, helping Copilot maintain coherence. It is session-scoped and not shared or persistent.

q: What is the benefit of including a specific function signature in a Copilot prompt?
opts: It reduces the token count of the response by providing a compressed structural hint
It gives Copilot structural context — parameter types, return type, naming — for a compatible implementation
It disables Copilot's fallback suggestions and requires it to match the exact signature provided
It forces Copilot to generate code only in the language specified in the signature's syntax
exp: Including a function signature gives Copilot concrete structural context — parameter types, return type, naming conventions — leading to more accurate implementations.

q: A developer provides one example input-output pair before asking Copilot to generate similar code. What technique is being used?
opts: System prompting
Zero-shot prompting
Few-shot prompting
One-shot prompting
exp: One-shot prompting provides exactly one example to guide the model. It is more targeted than zero-shot but less guided than few-shot.

q: How does GitHub Copilot determine which files and code to include in the context sent to the model?
opts: Open tabs, the active file, recent edits, and imports are used as relevance signals
The developer must manually pin files to include them as context
Every file in the repository is included alphabetically up to the context limit
Only the file currently active in the editor tab is ever included
exp: Copilot uses intelligent context selection based on relevance signals: open tabs, the current file, edit history, and imports — not simply all files.

q: When a developer sends a prompt to GitHub Copilot, where is the proxy server that processes the request located?
opts: On the organisation's private cloud infrastructure, behind their corporate firewall
Inside the AI model infrastructure, co-located with the GPU compute nodes
On the developer's local machine, inside the IDE extension process
At GitHub's servers, between the developer's IDE and the underlying AI model
exp: GitHub runs a proxy server that sits between the IDE and the LLM. It handles filtering, telemetry, and policy enforcement.

q: What is the purpose of the toxicity filter in GitHub Copilot's processing pipeline?
opts: It filters prompts or suggestions containing harmful, offensive, or unsafe content
It removes duplicate lines of code from suggestions to keep outputs concise
It blocks suggestions that closely match code found in public GitHub repositories
It prevents credentials and API keys from appearing in generated suggestions
exp: The toxicity filter screens both input prompts and output suggestions for harmful or inappropriate content as part of the responsible AI pipeline.

q: What does GitHub Copilot's post-processing step do after the model returns a suggestion?
opts: It sends the suggestion to the repository's CI pipeline to validate it before showing
It commits the accepted code directly to the active branch on behalf of the developer
It emails a copy of the suggestion to the organisation admin for review
It applies toxicity, duplication, and security filters to the raw LLM output before display
exp: Post-processing applies further filters to raw model output before the suggestion is shown in the IDE.

q: What does it mean when GitHub Copilot documentation refers to 'proxy filtering'?
opts: Routing all developer traffic through a corporate VPN before it reaches GitHub's servers
Server-side pre- and post-processing of prompts and responses to enforce safety and policy rules
Blocking all network traffic originating from outside the organisation's approved IP ranges
Encrypting suggestion content client-side before transmitting it to the IDE for display
exp: Proxy filtering refers to GitHub's server-side layer applying toxicity, duplication, and policy checks both before prompts reach the LLM and after the model responds.

q: Which of the following best describes a Large Language Model (LLM) as used by GitHub Copilot?
opts: A rule-based search engine that matches code patterns against a curated snippet database
A compiler extension that performs real-time correctness checking on partially written code
A database of pre-approved code templates selected and ranked by GitHub's engineering team
A neural network trained on large text and code corpora that predicts likely next tokens
exp: An LLM is a neural network trained on large corpora of text/code. It generates probabilistic predictions, not rule-based lookups or pre-stored snippets.

q: Where is the GitHub Copilot proxy server located relative to the developer's workflow?
opts: Between the developer's IDE and the internet
Between the AI model and GitHub's code storage
On the developer's local device as part of the IDE extension
Between the developer's IDE and the AI model, on GitHub's infrastructure
exp: The proxy sits between the IDE client and the underlying AI model on GitHub's infrastructure. It is not local and not at the storage layer.

q: Which two processes occur in the prompt-building phase before a request is sent to the LLM? (Select 2)
opts: Relevant context is assembled from editor signals, and outgoing prompts are filtered for safety
The IDE extension compiles a dependency graph of the repository before forwarding the request
The duplication filter compares the assembled prompt against known public code patterns
The model generates an initial draft suggestion, which is then reviewed for safety
exp: Before reaching the LLM, context is assembled and outgoing prompts are checked for harmful content. The model hasn't responded yet, so suggestion generation and output-side duplication checks happen after.

q: A developer is concerned about data privacy. Under GitHub Copilot Business, which statement about prompt data is accurate?
opts: Prompts are encrypted and stored in the organisation's private GitHub-managed cloud
Prompts are not retained after the suggestion is returned — they are discarded server-side
Prompts are stored for 28 days to support debugging and abuse detection
Prompts are forwarded to a third-party AI provider and retained for model improvement
exp: For Business/Enterprise, prompts are not retained post-response. They are used only to generate the suggestion, then discarded — this is a key data handling guarantee.

q: Which interaction mode should a developer use for quick, conversational questions about a specific piece of code without modifying files?
opts: Edit mode
Ask mode
Plan mode
Agent mode
exp: Ask mode is for conversational queries. Edit mode targets specific code changes; Plan mode creates multi-step strategies; Agent mode handles autonomous multi-file execution.

q: A developer needs to refactor a feature spanning 12 files with coordinated changes across the codebase. Which mode is most appropriate?
opts: Plan mode
Agent mode
Ask mode
Edit mode
exp: Agent mode provides autonomous reasoning and execution across multiple files for complex, multi-file tasks.

q: What is the key distinction between Plan mode and Agent mode?
opts: Plan mode creates structured multi-step strategies for human review; Agent mode autonomously executes code changes
Plan mode requires an Enterprise licence; Agent mode is available on all plans
Plan mode works only in VS Code; Agent mode works in all IDEs
Plan mode generates code; Agent mode only explains it
exp: Plan mode produces a strategy for the developer to review before any changes. Agent mode goes further and can autonomously write, edit, and apply changes across files.

q: What is the purpose of a `.github/copilot-instructions.md` file?
opts: It configures the Copilot licence tier and seat count for the repository
It provides persistent custom instructions to Copilot Chat for all interactions in the repository
It lists file paths that Copilot should treat as excluded from suggestions
It defines which IDE extensions are permitted for use alongside Copilot
exp: copilot-instructions.md lets teams embed custom context — coding standards, conventions, domain knowledge — that Copilot Chat uses for all interactions in the repository.

q: What is GitHub Copilot's Pull Request Summaries feature?
opts: An AI-generated summary describing the changes, context, and potential impact of a pull request
A report listing all Copilot suggestions that were accepted during the PR's development
An automatically generated code review checklist based on the repository's contributing guidelines
A tool that automatically merges pull requests that receive a passing Copilot review
exp: PR Summaries uses AI to draft a natural language description of what changed and why, helping reviewers understand pull requests more quickly.

q: What are MCP servers in the context of GitHub Copilot Agent mode?
opts: Managed Cloud Providers that host Copilot's AI model
Monitoring servers that track developer productivity
Security servers that scan Copilot suggestions for malware
Model Context Protocol servers that extend Agent mode with external tools and data sources
exp: MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers allow Agent mode to connect to external tools and data sources, extending what the agent can do beyond the local codebase.

q: What is GitHub Spark?
opts: A performance profiling tool for Copilot suggestions
A plugin for integrating Copilot with Slack
A GitHub Actions workflow that runs Copilot in CI/CD pipelines
An AI-powered tool for building small web apps using natural language
exp: GitHub Spark lets users describe an application in natural language and have AI generate and deploy a simple web app — targeting non-developers or rapid prototyping.

q: What is GitHub Copilot Spaces?
opts: A cloud storage feature for code snippets
A repository analytics dashboard
A collaborative workspace where teams can share Copilot context and instructions
A container environment for running Copilot-generated code
exp: Spaces is a feature that lets teams create shared Copilot environments with shared context and instructions, enabling more consistent AI-assisted collaboration.

q: Which two of the following are valid ways to trigger GitHub Copilot inline suggestions in the IDE? (Select 2)
opts: By right-clicking and selecting 'Generate with Copilot'
By typing code — suggestions appear automatically as you write
By pressing Alt+\\ (or Option+\\) to manually trigger a suggestion
By running git commit with a --copilot flag
exp: Copilot suggests inline automatically as you type, and can be manually triggered with Alt+\\ (Windows/Linux) or Option+\\ (Mac).

q: When would a developer use Edit mode instead of Ask mode in Copilot Chat?
opts: When they want a conversational explanation of a concept
When they want to make targeted code changes directly in the file
When they want to plan a complex multi-file refactoring
When they want Copilot to autonomously fix bugs across the codebase
exp: Edit mode is designed for targeted, direct code modifications — the developer specifies what to change, and Copilot makes the edit in place. Ask mode is for Q&A without file modification.

q: A developer uses Copilot for code review. What kind of feedback does Copilot provide?
opts: It automatically approves or rejects pull requests on behalf of the reviewer
It runs code in a sandboxed environment and reports runtime errors directly
It suggests improvements and flags issues, but the developer must review its feedback before acting
It generates a legally binding code review report that supersedes human review
exp: Copilot code review provides AI-generated suggestions and observations. Like all AI output, its feedback requires human review — it does not auto-approve or take final action.

q: What is the purpose of Sub-Agents in GitHub Copilot Agent mode?
opts: Junior developer accounts with limited Copilot access granted by the org admin
Sub-Agents are delegated tasks within a session to optimise context and parallelise work
Monitoring processes that alert admins when token usage approaches plan limits
Backup models activated when the primary model is unavailable or rate-limited
exp: Sub-Agents in Agent mode allow tasks to be delegated to specialised agents within a session, helping manage context window usage and parallelise complex tasks.

q: How do prompt files (`.github/prompts/`) differ from copilot-instructions.md?
opts: Prompt files are only usable in the CLI; copilot-instructions.md is IDE-only
Prompt files are reusable task-specific templates; copilot-instructions.md provides always-on repo context
Prompt files always override copilot-instructions.md when both are present in the repo
Both serve identical purposes and can be used interchangeably
exp: Prompt files are task-specific, reusable templates (e.g. a 'write unit tests' prompt) that can be invoked on demand. copilot-instructions.md is always-active context for the whole repo.

q: What is the correct sequence to start using GitHub Copilot CLI for the first time after installation?
opts: gh auth login then open browser to authenticate then gh copilot start
gh copilot suggest then gh auth login then trust folder
Trust the folder, then gh auth login, then browser opens automatically, then Copilot CLI is ready
npm install then gh copilot configure then gh auth login
exp: The CLI setup sequence confirmed by multiple exam takers: trust the folder, then gh auth login, browser opens automatically for authentication, then Copilot CLI is ready.

q: Which command is used to ask GitHub Copilot CLI for help constructing a shell command?
opts: gh copilot ask
gh copilot suggest
gh copilot run
gh copilot explain
exp: 'gh copilot suggest' asks Copilot to suggest a shell command. 'gh copilot explain' explains a given command.

q: You are in a CLI session under /root/projectA and need to trust the folder /root/projectB without leaving the current session. What should you do?
opts: Exit the session, navigate to /root/projectB, then run gh copilot trust
Edit ~/.gitconfig to add the trusted path
Run gh copilot trust /root/projectB from within the current session
Open a new terminal tab and navigate to /root/projectB
exp: You can trust a different folder from within an active CLI session by providing the target path: 'gh copilot trust /root/projectB'. No need to exit.

q: What does `gh copilot explain` do?
opts: Opens GitHub Copilot Chat in the browser
Provides a natural language explanation of a given shell command
Generates a new shell script based on a description
Authenticates the CLI session with GitHub
exp: 'gh copilot explain' takes a shell command and provides a natural language explanation of what it does — useful for understanding unfamiliar commands.

q: After installing the GitHub CLI extension for Copilot, which base command is used to interact with Copilot from the terminal?
opts: gh copilot
github copilot
git copilot
copilot
exp: The correct command prefix is 'gh copilot'. The GitHub CLI uses 'gh' as the base, with 'copilot' as the extension sub-command.

q: A developer is in a Copilot CLI interactive session and wants to generate a bash script. Which command starts this process?
opts: gh copilot generate
gh copilot suggest --script
gh copilot suggest
gh copilot script
exp: 'gh copilot suggest' is the command for requesting command or script suggestions in the CLI. The type of output is selected interactively.

q: An organisation admin wants to prevent developers from using GitHub Copilot in a specific IDE. Where should this be configured?
opts: In the Enterprise GitHub dashboard only
In each developer's IDE settings
In the repository's .github folder
In the Organisation-level Copilot policy settings under feature availability
exp: Organisation-level Copilot policy settings include controls for which IDEs and surfaces Copilot features are available on.

q: What is the cascade logic for GitHub Copilot configuration levels?
opts: Individual settings always override organisation settings
A lower level can never grant permissions that a higher level has blocked
Organisation settings only apply to Enterprise plan users
A lower level can expand but never restrict what a higher level defines
exp: This is the core cascade rule: Enterprise > Organisation > Repository > Individual. A lower level cannot unlock something blocked at a higher level.

q: A new developer joins an organisation and their IDE is configured to show Copilot suggestions, but the organisation policy blocks Copilot in all IDEs. What happens?
opts: No suggestions are shown — the organisation policy overrides local settings
Copilot suggestions are shown but flagged as policy-violating
The developer's local IDE setting takes precedence
The developer is prompted to request an exception
exp: Organisation-level policies override individual/IDE-level settings. This is the cascade logic in action.

q: Which two statements correctly describe how GitHub Copilot code review policies work? (Select 2)
opts: Custom review standards can be defined using instructions files
Code review policies can only be applied at the repository level, not org-wide
Admins can enable Copilot as an automatic reviewer on pull requests
Copilot Code Review replaces all human reviewers
exp: Admins can configure Copilot as an automatic reviewer, and custom standards can be set via instructions files. Human review is still expected; policies can be applied org-wide.

q: An Enterprise admin blocks GitHub Copilot usage on github.com for all members. A Business unit admin tries to re-enable it for their team. What is the outcome?
opts: The Business unit admin can override the Enterprise policy
The setting is undefined until GitHub support intervenes
The Enterprise policy takes precedence — Copilot on github.com remains blocked
The individual user's preference determines the outcome
exp: Enterprise-level policies are the highest level and cannot be overridden by lower levels (organisation, team, individual).

q: Where can a GitHub organisation admin view and manage current Copilot seat assignments?
opts: In the Enterprise billing dashboard only
In the repository settings for each project
In the Organisation settings under GitHub Copilot > Access
In each developer's personal profile settings
exp: Copilot seat assignments are managed under Organisation settings > GitHub Copilot > Access. This is also where policies and exclusions are configured.

q: Which two of the following are well-supported use cases for GitHub Copilot improving developer productivity? (Select 2)
opts: Generating boilerplate code and repetitive patterns
Generating unit tests for existing functions
Making autonomous architecture decisions without developer input
Approving and merging pull requests automatically
exp: Copilot excels at boilerplate generation and unit test creation. Autonomous architecture decisions and PR merges require human judgment.

q: A team wants to use GitHub Copilot to modernise a legacy Python 2 codebase to Python 3. Which Copilot capability is most relevant?
opts: Audit log review to identify which developers introduced the deprecated Python 2 patterns
Pull Request summaries to document what the legacy code originally did before migration
Content exclusion configuration to prevent the legacy code from being used as context
Refactoring suggestions for modernising legacy code to updated equivalents
exp: Copilot can assist with legacy code modernisation by suggesting refactored, updated equivalents.

q: How does GitHub Copilot help reduce context switching for developers?
opts: It blocks distracting websites during coding sessions to reduce switching
It provides in-editor answers and explanations, eliminating the need to leave the IDE
It automatically opens relevant documentation tabs in a side-by-side browser panel
It syncs IDE state and cursor position across multiple monitors for continuity
exp: By answering questions, explaining code, and suggesting implementations in-editor, Copilot reduces the need to switch to browsers, documentation sites, or Stack Overflow.

q: A developer asks Copilot to generate sample test data for a database migration script. Which Copilot capability is this?
opts: Pull Request summarisation
Sample data generation
Duplication detection
Content exclusion
exp: Sample data generation is an explicit Copilot productivity feature — it can generate realistic dummy/test data structures based on schema or context.

q: Which of the following best describes how Copilot accelerates learning for junior developers?
opts: It generates completion certificates that track and validate junior developer progress
It provides contextual explanations and examples inline, helping juniors learn patterns while working
It promotes junior developers automatically when their suggestion acceptance rate exceeds a threshold
It replaces the need for senior mentorship entirely by answering all coding questions autonomously
exp: Copilot helps junior developers learn by providing contextual code examples and explanations inline, reducing the learning curve for unfamiliar APIs or patterns.

q: What is a key benefit of using GitHub Copilot for unit test generation?
opts: It guarantees 100% code coverage
It can quickly generate test cases including edge cases, reducing repetitive test writing
It replaces the need for a dedicated QA team
It automatically runs and deploys tests to production
exp: Copilot accelerates test writing by generating test cases (including edge cases) but still requires developer review. It does not guarantee coverage or replace QA.

q: GitHub Copilot can flag potential security vulnerabilities in suggested code. Which statement best describes this capability?
opts: It runs a full SAST scan on every commit and blocks merges when vulnerabilities are detected
It integrates with CVE databases to apply real-time patches to insecure suggestions automatically
It enforces compliance with all applicable regulatory frameworks for the detected language
It identifies common vulnerability patterns like SQL injection or hardcoded secrets and suggests safer alternatives
exp: Copilot recognises common vulnerability patterns and suggests improvements, but it is not a full SAST tool.

q: Which two of the following best describe limitations of AI-generated unit tests? (Select 2)
opts: Generated tests require developer review to ensure they test the right behaviour
Tests may not cover all meaningful edge cases without developer guidance
Copilot cannot generate tests for any language other than JavaScript
Tests are always syntactically incorrect
exp: AI-generated tests can miss edge cases and may test incorrect assumptions. Developer review is always required. Copilot supports many languages.

q: A developer uses Copilot to generate code that queries a database. The suggestion does not sanitise user input. What should the developer do?
opts: Report the suggestion to GitHub and wait for a fix
Disable Copilot's security features and use the raw suggestion
Review and modify the suggestion to include proper input sanitisation before committing
Accept the suggestion since Copilot's security filtering will catch issues at runtime
exp: Developers must review and fix security issues in AI-generated code. Copilot's filters are not a substitute for developer security review.

q: What does GitHub Copilot's security warning feature do?
opts: Emails the security team when a risky suggestion is accepted
Highlights potentially insecure code patterns in suggestions and prompts the developer to review them
Automatically patches known CVEs in the codebase
Blocks all code changes until a security audit is completed
exp: Security warnings flag potentially risky code patterns in suggestions, prompting developer review — not auto-patching.

q: Which of the following is the most accurate description of how GitHub Copilot handles intellectual property concerns in its suggestions?
opts: Copilot's training data consists exclusively of code under permissive Apache licences
GitHub provides full indemnification against IP claims arising from Copilot output
All Copilot suggestions are guaranteed to be original and free of IP concerns
Copilot uses a duplication filter to flag potential matches, but review is still the developer's responsibility
exp: The duplication filter is a mitigation tool, not a guarantee. Developers still bear responsibility for reviewing suggestions for potential IP issues.

q: In the context of GitHub Copilot, who is primarily accountable for AI-generated code that is deployed to production?
opts: The organisation's legal department
The developer who accepted and committed the suggestion
The AI model itself
The GitHub engineering team
exp: The developer who accepts, reviews, and commits AI-generated code is accountable for it. AI systems are not legal entities capable of bearing accountability.

q: Which term describes the responsible AI principle ensuring AI systems can be understood and scrutinised by stakeholders?
opts: Fairness
Accountability
Security
Transparency
exp: Transparency means AI systems and their decision-making can be understood and examined. It is distinct from accountability (who is responsible) and fairness (unbiased outputs).

q: A team discovers that Copilot suggestions for financial calculations contain systematic rounding errors. What responsible AI concept does this illustrate?
opts: Insufficient context was provided in the prompt for accurate financial calculation
The duplication filter incorrectly matched the calculation to a different public formula
Insufficient GPU resources caused approximation errors in the underlying model
LLM hallucination — generating plausible but incorrect output that requires human validation
exp: LLM hallucination — generating plausible but incorrect output — is a core limitation. This illustrates why human validation of AI-generated code is non-negotiable.

q: Which two of the following reflect the principle of 'security' in responsible AI use of GitHub Copilot? (Select 2)
opts: Reviewing AI-generated code for potential security vulnerabilities before deployment
Assuming AI-generated code is secure because GitHub's filters are comprehensive
Deploying AI-generated code without penetration testing to save time
Using Copilot's security warning feature as one layer of a broader security practice
exp: Security in responsible AI means proactive review and using Copilot's warnings as one tool among many — not relying solely on automated filters.

q: A developer uses Copilot to generate an image classification model. It performs poorly on under-represented demographic groups. Which responsible AI principle is most relevant?
opts: Fairness
Transparency
Security
Accountability
exp: Fairness addresses bias and equitable performance across groups. Poor performance on under-represented demographics is a classic fairness failure.

q: Which statement most accurately reflects the relationship between AI automation and human oversight in GitHub Copilot use?
opts: AI should handle all routine coding autonomously, freeing developers from review entirely
Human oversight is only required for security-sensitive code, not general application logic
Oversight is optional for experienced developers who understand the codebase well
AI augments developer work, but human oversight and final decisions remain essential throughout
exp: The core responsible AI principle is that AI augments human work but never replaces human judgment and oversight. This applies universally, not just to security code.

q: Which of the following best illustrates the 'validate AI output' principle when using GitHub Copilot?
opts: Running 'git blame' on AI-generated lines after merging
Executing a generated SQL query against the production database immediately to test it
Accepting suggestions only from trusted team members who use Copilot
Running the generated code through unit tests and code review before merging
exp: Validation means testing and reviewing before merging. Running untested code in production is the opposite of responsible validation.

q: Which two of the following best represent the principle of 'identifying potential harms' in responsible AI use of Copilot? (Select 2)
opts: Identifying cases where AI suggestions may perpetuate biased outcomes in code logic
Trusting that GitHub's legal team has reviewed all potential AI harms
Recognising that AI-generated code may introduce security vulnerabilities
Assuming that all Copilot suggestions are safe because they are filtered
exp: Responsible harm identification means recognising both security risks and fairness/bias risks in AI output.

q: Why should developers avoid using GitHub Copilot suggestions in safety-critical systems (e.g. medical devices) without extensive additional validation?
opts: LLMs can produce plausible but incorrect code, and safety-critical failures carry extreme consequences
Copilot is not licensed for use in any regulated industry by GitHub's terms
Copilot's suggestions are frozen at a past API version that predates current safety standards
GitHub's terms of service explicitly prohibit Copilot use in safety-critical systems
exp: LLM hallucination is a fundamental risk. In safety-critical contexts, the consequences of unvalidated errors are severe — extensive additional validation is required.

q: Which Copilot plan is appropriate for an individual open-source developer who wants AI-assisted coding without organisational controls?
opts: GitHub Copilot Enterprise
GitHub Copilot Free or Pro
GitHub Copilot Business
No plan supports individual open-source use
exp: Free and Pro plans are designed for individual developers. Business and Enterprise add organisational management capabilities not needed for solo use.

q: Which plan allows an admin to receive suggestions with GitHub Copilot on github.com while reviewing pull requests, with context from the organisation's private repositories?
opts: Copilot Business
Copilot Enterprise
Copilot Pro
Copilot Free
exp: Copilot Enterprise includes Copilot on github.com with private-repo context for activities like PR review. This is not available on Business or lower.

q: What is the minimum plan required to use Copilot for Pull Request code review on github.com?
opts: It defines the billing and renewal schedule for Copilot Business subscriptions
It explains how to set up Copilot in a new IDE environment step by step
It describes the git branching strategy used to review and merge AI-generated suggestions
It shows how keystrokes become a prompt, pass through GitHub's proxy and LLM, and return as a suggestion
exp: Copilot Code Review on github.com is an organisation-level feature requiring Business or Enterprise. Individual Free/Pro plans do not support this.

q: A developer on a Pro plan wants to enable organisation-wide content exclusions for their solo project. What should they do?
opts: Add the exclusion to the global IDE settings
Enable exclusions in the repository settings instead — this is sufficient for individual use
Contact GitHub support to enable it for Pro
Upgrade to Business or Enterprise to get org-level policy controls
exp: For an individual developer, repository-level content exclusions are the appropriate tool. Org-level controls require Business/Enterprise.

q: Which plan allows an admin to programmatically add and remove Copilot seats for their organisation via the REST API?
opts: Any plan supports REST API seat management
Copilot Free
Copilot Pro
Copilot Business or Enterprise
exp: REST API seat management is available for Business and Enterprise plan administrators. It is not available on Free or Pro.

q: Which two of the following are included in ALL paid Copilot plans (Pro, Business, Enterprise)? (Select 2)
opts: Fine-tuned models on private code
Organisation-level policy management
Inline code suggestions in the IDE
GitHub Copilot Chat
exp: Inline suggestions and Copilot Chat are core features available across all paid plans. Policy management is Business/Enterprise only; fine-tuned models are Enterprise only.

q: A developer on the Free plan reaches the monthly Copilot usage limit. What happens?
opts: Copilot is permanently disabled for that account
The developer must contact GitHub support to continue
Copilot suggestions stop until the limit resets or the developer upgrades to a paid plan
The developer is automatically upgraded to Pro
exp: The Free plan has usage limits. When reached, suggestions stop until the limit resets (typically monthly) or the developer upgrades to Pro or higher.

q: Which Copilot plan is best for a 500-person company needing org-level governance, audit logs, and policy enforcement, but NOT requiring fine-tuned models or private-repo Chat on github.com?
opts: Copilot Business
Copilot Free
Copilot Pro
Copilot Enterprise
exp: Business meets all these needs: org governance, audit logs, policy enforcement. Enterprise adds fine-tuned models and private-repo Chat on github.com — not needed here.

q: An organisation wants to investigate whether a specific developer's Copilot access was revoked and re-granted. Where would this information be found?
opts: Copilot is offline due to a service outage affecting the developer's region
The file extension is not in the list of languages currently supported by Copilot in this IDE
The developer's current licence tier does not include suggestions for this file type
A content exclusion has been applied to that file at the repository or organisation level
exp: Seat assignment events (grant, revoke) are administrative actions recorded in the organisation audit log.

q: GitHub Copilot usage metrics can show which of the following?
opts: The exact prompts each developer sent to Copilot
The git commits that were written with Copilot's help
Individual developer productivity scores
Per-seat acceptance rates, active user counts, and suggestion volumes — but not prompt content
exp: Usage metrics surface aggregate stats like acceptance rates and active users. Prompt content is never exposed.

q: What is the difference between the Copilot audit log and Copilot usage metrics?
opts: They are the same underlying data, presented differently in the UI for different audiences
Audit logs capture administrative and policy events; usage metrics show aggregated activity statistics
Audit logs are only for Enterprise plans; usage metrics are available on Business plans only
Usage metrics record every developer keystroke; audit logs record only system-level errors
exp: Audit logs = administrative events (seat changes, policy changes). Usage metrics = aggregated activity data (acceptance rates, active users). They serve different purposes.

q: Which two types of events would appear in the GitHub Copilot organisation audit log? (Select 2)
opts: A manager enabling Copilot for a new team member
A Copilot suggestion being accepted by a developer
A developer opening a file that is excluded from Copilot
An admin updating the content exclusion policy
exp: Audit logs record administrative actions: enabling/disabling access for members, and policy changes. They do not record suggestion acceptance or file-opening events.

q: A compliance officer asks for evidence that no developer's code prompts were retained by GitHub Copilot Business. What documentation supports this?
opts: Individual developers' IDE telemetry logs exported from their local machines
The organisation's git commit history showing no AI-attributed commits
GitHub's data handling policy for Business/Enterprise, which explicitly states prompts are not retained
The usage metrics dashboard showing zero retained prompts in the current period
exp: GitHub's official data handling policy for Business/Enterprise states that prompts are not retained. This policy documentation is the correct reference for compliance.

q: Which of the following events would NOT be found in the GitHub Copilot organisation audit log?
opts: An admin changing the public code matching (duplication) policy
A developer's suggestion acceptance rate dropping below 20%
An admin enabling Copilot for the entire organisation
A seat being removed from a specific team member
exp: Audit logs record administrative events — policy changes, seat assignments. Suggestion acceptance rates are usage metrics, not audit log entries.

q: A developer excluded a path at the repository level but the org admin has not defined any exclusion for it. Can other org members working on a different repository see Copilot suggestions for that path?
opts: Yes — repository-level exclusions only apply to users working within that specific repository
It depends on each developer's IDE settings
No — repository exclusions propagate to all org members
No — all exclusions are global across the org
exp: Repository-level exclusions are scoped to that repository only. Members in other repositories are unaffected.

q: A repository admin wants to define a content exclusion that applies only to that repository, not the whole organisation. Where should the exclusion be defined?
opts: It has no effect — Copilot only reads executable code tokens and skips comment blocks entirely
It triggers the few-shot learning pipeline, registering the comment as a new training example
It serves as a natural prompt, giving Copilot rich context to generate a well-targeted implementation
It automatically disables Copilot suggestions for that function to prevent conflicting with the spec
exp: Repository-level content exclusions are configured in the repository settings, under the Copilot section. They apply only to that repository.

q: A developer notices Copilot is not offering suggestions in a file containing proprietary algorithms. No error is shown. What is the most likely reason?
opts: The file extension is not in the list of supported languages for the current IDE version
The developer's current seat assignment does not include access to suggestions for that directory
Copilot is temporarily offline and will resume suggestions when the service is restored
A content exclusion has been applied to that file at the repository or organisation level
exp: Silent absence of suggestions with no error is the expected behaviour when a content exclusion is active. Copilot does not alert the developer — it simply withholds suggestions.

q: A developer disables Copilot for a specific file via their local IDE settings. An org-level policy also excludes that file. What is the effective state?
opts: Both exclusions apply — the file is excluded regardless of which level is checked
Only the org setting applies; IDE settings are redundant
Only the IDE setting applies; org settings are ignored locally
The settings conflict and Copilot shows an error
exp: Exclusions are additive. Whether a file is excluded via IDE, repo, or org settings, the result is the same: Copilot will not use it or suggest within it.

q: Which file is used to provide repository-specific custom instructions to GitHub Copilot Chat?
opts: .github/copilot-ignore
.github/copilot-instructions.md
.copilotrc in the repository root
copilot.config.json alongside the package manifest
exp: .github/copilot-instructions.md is the designated file for repository-level custom instructions that shape Copilot Chat's behaviour for all users in that repo.

q: A developer sees that Copilot is not suggesting code in a file they expect to work with. No error message is shown. How should they investigate?
opts: Check for content exclusions at repository and organisation level that may cover that file
Update the Copilot plan tier, as suggestion limits may have been reached for this billing period
Clear the IDE cache and restart — stale cached policies can suppress suggestions silently
Reinstall the IDE extension, as missing suggestions usually indicate a corrupted install
exp: Silent absence of suggestions is the expected behaviour for excluded files. The developer should check repository and org-level content exclusion settings.

q: An admin wants Copilot to enforce specific coding standards automatically during code review. Which approach supports this?
opts: Edit the LLM training data with the standards
Use a .copilotignore file to reference the standards document
Configure the standards in each developer's IDE settings
Define review standards in a Copilot instructions file associated with code review policies
exp: Custom review standards are defined in instructions files that Copilot Code Review uses, allowing consistent, standards-based automated review feedback.

q: An org admin enables Copilot for all members. Two weeks later, a specific developer's access stops working. What is the most likely administrative cause?
opts: The developer's IDE is incompatible
Copilot is down for maintenance
The developer's seat was revoked, which would appear in the audit log
Copilot automatically expires after 14 days
exp: Seat revocation is the most likely administrative cause. This event would be logged in the organisation's Copilot audit log.

q: A developer at a Business plan company uses Copilot in JetBrains IDE. The org admin disabled Copilot in all IDEs except VS Code. What happens?
opts: Copilot works but logs a warning to the audit log
Copilot works normally since the developer has a valid licence
Copilot is blocked — the org policy restricting IDE usage takes precedence
JetBrains prompts the developer to upgrade their plan
exp: Org-level policies override individual preferences. If the org has disabled Copilot outside VS Code, it will not function in JetBrains regardless of the developer's personal settings.

q: An admin configures content exclusions at both the organisation level and repository level for the same path. What is the net effect?
opts: Both settings apply additively — the path is excluded regardless of which level is checked
The organisation-level setting is ignored if a repository-level one exists
The repository-level setting overwrites the organisation-level one
A conflict error is raised and both settings are disabled
exp: Exclusions from multiple levels are additive. Multiple levels excluding the same path simply reinforce each other — there is no conflict or override.

q: What is the role of the 'code suggestion lifecycle' in understanding GitHub Copilot?
opts: It explains the steps required to set up Copilot in a new IDE for the first time
It shows how keystrokes become a prompt, pass through GitHub's proxy and LLM, and return as a filtered suggestion
It outlines the billing and renewal cycle for Copilot Business subscriptions
It describes the git workflow for committing and reviewing Copilot-generated code
exp: The code suggestion lifecycle traces the full path: keystroke → context assembly → proxy → LLM → post-processing → suggestion displayed.

q: What does GitHub Copilot use as the primary mechanism to tailor suggestions to the current codebase?
opts: Pre-trained knowledge of every public GitHub repository indexed at training time
A static full-repo index built once when the project is first opened in the IDE
The context window, assembled dynamically from open files, edits, and imports per request
A dedicated fine-tuned model that is updated whenever new commits are pushed to the repo
exp: Copilot uses the context window — dynamically assembled from open files, edit history, and imports — as the primary mechanism for tailoring suggestions.

q: What is the significance of GitHub Copilot's use of a context window rather than having access to the full repository?
opts: It makes Copilot cheaper to run by reducing the amount of code processed
Copilot selects a relevant subset of code that fits the window, so large repos can't be fully referenced at once
It has no practical impact — Copilot effectively sees the whole project anyway
Suggestions are limited strictly to functions visible in the active file
exp: The context window is a fundamental LLM constraint. Copilot intelligently selects what fits within it, but cannot reference every file in a large repo simultaneously.

q: What happens to a developer's prompt after GitHub Copilot Business returns a suggestion?
opts: It is archived in the audit log
It is discarded — not retained after the API call completes
It is stored for 28 days for debugging purposes
It is anonymised and used to improve the model
exp: Under Business/Enterprise, prompts are not retained after the suggestion is returned.

q: Which two of the following are limitations of LLMs that affect GitHub Copilot's suggestion quality? (Select 2)
opts: LLMs may reflect biases present in training data
LLMs have perfect knowledge of all programming languages
LLMs always understand the business logic of the codebase
LLMs can generate plausible but factually incorrect code
exp: LLMs can hallucinate and may reflect biases in training data. They do not inherently understand business logic or have perfect language coverage.

q: Which of the following best explains why GitHub Copilot suggestions may sometimes use deprecated APIs?
opts: The developer's IDE is not connected to the internet and uses a cached suggestion set
The IDE extension has a dependency on an older SDK that references deprecated methods
Suggestions are intentionally limited to stable, older API versions for reliability
LLMs have a training data cutoff, so post-cutoff API changes won't appear in suggestions
exp: LLMs have a training data cutoff. Post-cutoff API deprecations won't be reflected in suggestions, making developer review essential for staying current.

q: What does 'input processing' refer to in GitHub Copilot's data flow?
opts: Parsing and tokenising developer keystrokes to optimise request latency and throughput
Assembling context, applying pre-filters, and building the structured prompt before sending to the LLM
Converting source files from text encoding to binary format before secure transmission to GitHub
Compiling the AI-generated code to verify it is syntactically correct before displaying it
exp: Input processing encompasses context assembly, pre-filtering (e.g. toxicity), and prompt construction — everything that happens before the LLM receives the request.

q: Why does GitHub Copilot not use the entire repository as context for every suggestion?
opts: Sending all files would violate the data privacy provisions of the Business plan agreement
Copilot is architecturally limited to processing only the single file currently in focus
Repository-wide access would require an Enterprise fine-tuned model to be cost-effective
LLMs have a finite context window, so only a selected relevant subset of code can be included
exp: LLMs have a context window limit. Copilot intelligently selects the most relevant content to fit within it, rather than including everything.

q: What is the role of the prompt builder in GitHub Copilot's architecture?
opts: The IDE extension, which packages the raw active file and sends it unchanged to GitHub
The duplication filter, which pre-processes context to remove any publicly matching code
The component that assembles context from open files, tabs, and signals into a structured prompt
The LLM itself, which queries the repository index directly to self-assemble relevant context
exp: The prompt builder assembles relevant context into the structured prompt before it reaches the LLM.

q: A developer is concerned that Copilot might leak secrets from one project to another via the model's memory. Why is this NOT a risk with GitHub Copilot Business?
opts: Copilot Business uses a fully isolated model instance per organisation to prevent cross-contamination
GitHub encrypts all context before sending it, so the model cannot read raw code
Secrets are automatically stripped from context by the IDE extension before any data leaves the machine
Prompts are discarded after each response — the model has no persistent memory between sessions
exp: Because prompts are not retained and the model has no persistent session memory, data from one project cannot leak to another via Copilot Business.

q: What is the benefit of referencing specific files or symbols in a Copilot Chat prompt (e.g. using #file or @workspace)?
opts: It disables Copilot's safety filters for that session
It forces Copilot to use a specific programming language
It narrows and focuses the context Copilot uses, leading to more accurate and relevant answers
It increases the token limit of the response
exp: Using context references like #file or @workspace tells Copilot exactly what to focus on, improving answer relevance and reducing hallucinations.

q: Why might a poorly worded prompt lead to unhelpful Copilot suggestions?
opts: Vague prompts give Copilot insufficient signal, leading to generic or off-target suggestions
Copilot charges additional tokens when it has to interpret unclear intent
Short prompts trigger the safety filter and are blocked before reaching the model
Copilot rejects ambiguous prompts automatically and returns a structured error
exp: Copilot's output quality is directly tied to prompt quality. Vague, ambiguous prompts lack the context needed for targeted, useful suggestions.

q: A developer writes a detailed comment above an empty function, describing expected inputs, outputs, and edge cases. How does this help Copilot?
opts: It has no effect — Copilot reads only executable code and ignores all comment blocks
It automatically triggers the few-shot learning pipeline, using the comment as a training example
It disables inline suggestions for the function block to prevent conflicting with the spec
It acts as a natural prompt, giving Copilot rich context to generate an accurate implementation
exp: Detailed comments above functions serve as natural prompts. Copilot reads them as context and uses them to inform the generated implementation.

q: A developer writes: 'Refactor this function to follow the Single Responsibility Principle and add JSDoc comments.' What makes this an effective prompt?
opts: It is specific about both the refactoring goal (SRP) and the expected output (JSDoc comments)
It uses terminology that Copilot's training has specifically optimised it to recognise
It includes a role assignment that tells the model to act as a refactoring specialist
It is short enough to process quickly, which improves response time significantly
exp: Effective prompts are specific about what to do (refactor to SRP) and what to produce (JSDoc comments). Specificity directly improves suggestion relevance.

q: When should a developer use few-shot prompting over zero-shot prompting with GitHub Copilot?
opts: When the desired output pattern is easier to demonstrate by example than to describe in words
When the prompt needs to be as short as possible to stay within token limits
When the user is interacting with Copilot CLI rather than the IDE chat interface
When the task is simple enough that a single instruction is sufficient without examples
exp: Few-shot prompting is most valuable when the output format or pattern is complex and easier to show through examples than to describe precisely in words.

q: Which two elements make a Copilot Chat prompt more effective? (Select 2)
opts: Using passive voice to seem more polite
Including example inputs and expected outputs
Using only single-word prompts for clarity
Specifying the desired output format (e.g. 'return as a JSON object')
exp: Examples (few-shot context) and explicit format instructions both improve prompt effectiveness. Single-word prompts lack specificity; voice/politeness does not affect AI output quality.

q: A developer wants Copilot to output a function that returns a specific error type on failure. How should they phrase the prompt?
opts: Explicitly state the error type and conditions in the prompt, e.g. 'Return a ValueError if input is negative'
Just describe the happy path and let Copilot figure out error handling
Use zero-shot prompting and accept whatever Copilot suggests for errors
Ask in a second prompt after the function is generated
exp: Explicitly specifying error handling behaviour in the prompt is more effective than relying on Copilot to infer it. Specificity in prompts directly improves output accuracy.

q: How does GitHub Copilot help developers when working with an unfamiliar API or library?
opts: It downloads and installs the missing library automatically into the active project environment
It generates inline usage examples and explains API methods, reducing the need for external docs
It only generates code for libraries that are part of Copilot's pre-approved integration set
It blocks suggestions involving any library not already present in the repository's dependency file
exp: Copilot can generate example usage and explain APIs inline, helping developers learn and use unfamiliar libraries without leaving the editor.

q: Which of the following best describes how Copilot helps with documentation generation?
opts: It generates docstrings, inline comments, and README content based on the code being analysed
It validates all generated documentation against an ISO technical writing standard automatically
It publishes generated documentation directly to GitHub Pages as part of the commit workflow
It provides instant translation of all generated documentation into 50 supported spoken languages
exp: Copilot can generate docstrings, inline comments, and README content based on code analysis.

q: A developer is debugging an unfamiliar error. They paste the error message and stack trace into Copilot Chat. What is Copilot most likely to provide?
opts: An automated patch applied directly to the failing code after diagnosing the root cause
An explanation of the error and suggested fixes or debugging approaches based on the stack trace
A list of all developers who may have contributed to the error based on git blame analysis
A request to access production logs or monitoring dashboards for more complete runtime context
exp: Copilot Chat is well-suited to error analysis — it can interpret error messages and stack traces to explain what went wrong and suggest potential fixes.

q: In which way does GitHub Copilot help developers working with legacy codebases?
opts: Relevant files demonstrating the existing naming conventions must be open as context
Copilot must have been pre-trained specifically on that codebase by GitHub engineering
A copilot-instructions.md file must explicitly enumerate all naming patterns and rules
The developer must be on an Enterprise plan with fine-tuning enabled for their org
exp: Copilot's legacy modernisation capabilities include explaining old code, suggesting updated implementations, and guiding incremental migration.

q: A developer asks Copilot to suggest variable names that follow the codebase's naming conventions. What must be true for Copilot to do this well?
opts: Copilot must have been fine-tuned on the codebase
A copilot-instructions.md file must explicitly list all naming rules
The relevant files demonstrating naming conventions must be open as context
The developer must be on an Enterprise plan
exp: Copilot learns naming conventions from context — open files showing existing patterns help it match the codebase's style.

q: Which Copilot feature is most useful for a developer who has just joined a project and needs to understand the existing codebase quickly?
opts: Content exclusions — to prevent Copilot from accessing sensitive legacy modules
Copilot Chat — to ask questions about unfamiliar code and receive inline explanations
Pull Request summaries — to get an overview of recent changes to the codebase
Duplication detection — to check if similar code already exists in the codebase
exp: Copilot Chat allows new developers to ask questions about unfamiliar code and get explanations, significantly accelerating onboarding.

q: How does GitHub Copilot's ability to generate sample data benefit database developers?
opts: It creates automated database backups by cloning production data for local testing
It validates generated data against database constraints and schema rules automatically
It inserts data directly into the connected database during the development session
It generates realistic, schema-aware seed data and INSERT statements to use in tests
exp: Copilot can generate schema-aware test data and seed scripts, saving developers significant time during development and testing phases.

q: A developer asks Copilot to refactor a function for better performance. Which Copilot capability is most directly used?
opts: Explaining what an existing shell command does in plain language
Generating and running Python notebooks interactively from the terminal
Helping interactively with git and gh CLI commands and workflows
Suggesting shell commands and scripts from a natural language description
exp: Refactoring for performance is a direct use of Copilot's refactoring capability — suggesting improved implementations of existing code.

q: A developer opens five related files as tabs before asking Copilot to help refactor a function. Why is this beneficial?
opts: It enables Copilot to autonomously create and apply a refactoring plan across all open files
Open tabs serve as context signals, helping Copilot generate suggestions compatible with related files
It is a prerequisite step required before Edit mode can process multi-file changes
It increases Copilot's token processing throughput by pre-caching file content
exp: Open tabs are used by Copilot as context signals. Having related files open increases the likelihood that suggestions will be compatible with the broader codebase.

q: A developer uses Copilot to generate integration tests. Which statement is most accurate about these tests?
opts: They are inherently more reliable than manually written tests because AI avoids human oversight bias
They are guaranteed to correctly simulate production system behaviour without further modification
They provide a useful starting point but require review to ensure they match actual system behaviour
They automatically connect to the staging database to use realistic data in integration scenarios
exp: AI-generated integration tests are a starting point. They require review to ensure they reflect actual integration points and infrastructure.

q: Which of the following is the most appropriate use of GitHub Copilot in a security-sensitive codebase?
opts: Use Copilot to generate initial implementations, then apply thorough security review before deployment
Use Copilot freely with no additional review since the toxicity filter handles security
Disable Copilot entirely — it is not suitable for security-sensitive projects
Let Copilot manage all security configurations autonomously
exp: Copilot is useful for productivity even in security-sensitive contexts, but its output always requires additional security review.
